paragraphs.text: This tuo of [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) is made from leaf grown in Menghai County, Yunnan. On a label, Menghai can mean the county or [Menghai Tea Factory](menghai-county:county-and-factory), which stands inside it and blends leaf from several of its mountains. Here the name says where the leaf grew, and no single mountain is given.

Before it was pressed, the leaf was wetted and heaped in a [wet pile](shou:wet-piling). The pile is covered to hold the heat its microbes make and turned about once a week to let air in. The method was built to give in weeks the change raw pu’er takes years of keeping to reach, so a ripe tuo is ready to drink soon after it is made. The county runs through that history: in 1973 its factory joined Kunming and Xiaguan in sending a team to learn piling in Guangzhou, and by 1975 [the Menghai method](shou:piling-1973) had settled into the ripe pu’er made today.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.
